 Darkness on the horizon: Why Nepal’s winter power supply hangs in balance 
 Namaraj Acharya 
 November 12, 2026 
 21 MIN READ 
 Devastation across the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi corridors has left Nepal reliant on cross-border imports and a strained Kulekhani reservoir to keep the lights on. 
 A 
 A+ 
 A- 
 content_copy 
 bookmark_border 
 KATHMANDU: Nepal has ended years of load-shedding and reached a stage where it exports electricity. However, with the onset of winter, the old problems of declining electricity generation, rising demand, and high dependency on imports from India are set to recur. This year’s monsoon floods and landslides have caused additional damage to hydropower projects and transmission infrastructure, further compounding the challenges in the energy sector.
 Although the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) states that it is preparing supply management to prevent load-shedding, winter electricity supply will depend on imports from India, the restoration of damaged structures, and the capacity of the transmission system.
 The tough test for a load-shedding-free Nepal 
 Nepal experienced daily power cuts of up to 18 hours for a long time. Shortages in electricity generation, weak transmission infrastructure, growing demand, and management issues affected the country’s economic and industrial activities. Industrial establishments could not operate at full capacity, and the general public had to endure hours of power outages in their daily lives.
 While generation is high when river water levels rise during the rainy season, generation shrinks as water levels drop in winter.
 The end of load-shedding in the Kathmandu Valley began on the day of Laxmi Puja on 30 October 2016. Subsequently, power supply gradually improved in other parts of the country as well. On 14 May 2018, it was declared that industrial zones were also free from load-shedding. Since then, Nepal has reached a position where it exports surplus electricity during the wet season to India and Bangladesh.
 This transformation is no ordinary achievement. Nepal, which at one time could not operate industries due to electricity shortages, has now created a situation where it must find markets when generation is high in the rainy season. But this achievement has another side as well. A large share of electricity generation in Nepal is based on river flow. While water flow in rivers increases during the rainy season, boosting generation, flow decreases in winter, causing generation to shrink.
 Consequently, Nepal, which exports electricity during the rainy season, has still not been able to eliminate the need to import large quantities of electricity from India during the winter. This winter, that dependency is projected to become even more challenging. With floods and landslides damaging projects and affecting transmission infrastructure, the prospect of meeting demand through domestic generation has grown weaker.
 According to the Nepal Electricity Authority, the country’s total installed electricity generation capacity has now reached 3,739.40 megawatts. Another roughly 320 megawatts of capacity is expected to be connected to the grid by mid-December. Total installed capacity is then estimated to reach approximately 4,059 megawatts.
 Domestic generation appears capable of covering less than half of total demand, leaving the remaining requirement to be fulfilled by electricity imports from India.
 However, installed capacity and the electricity available in winter are not the same thing. Installed capacity is the maximum electricity a project can generate under favorable conditions. When river flows decrease in winter, run-of-the-river projects cannot generate electricity at their full capacity. For this reason, the NEA estimates that even with an installed capacity of nearly 4,000 megawatts, domestic generation in winter will be limited to 1,218 megawatts.
 On the other hand, peak electricity demand is projected to reach between 2,250 and 2,300 megawatts. In other words, domestic generation appears capable of covering less than half of total demand. The remaining demand will have to be fulfilled by importing electricity from India.
 Shree Raj Shakya, a professor at the Center for Energy Studies under Tribhuvan University’s Institute of Engineering, has also pointed to this seasonal dependency of Nepal’s energy system as a policy challenge. According to him, while setting targets for hydropower generation and export, a practical strategy prioritizing domestic consumption is essential.
 Unless electricity availability in winter, transmission infrastructure capacity, and demand management are improved simultaneously, ensuring a regular supply remains difficult.
 “The current necessity is to make the strategy of providing electricity for domestic consumption more practical than targeting electricity exports,” Shakya states. According to him, as disaster risks grow for projects based on Himalayan rivers, the generation and export-oriented strategy must be reconsidered.
 This reveals the true state of Nepal’s energy security. While an increasing installed capacity is positive, ensuring a regular supply will remain difficult unless winter electricity availability, transmission infrastructure capacity, and demand management are improved simultaneously.
 Preparations to bring 1,154 megawatts from India 
 To meet winter demand, the Nepal Electricity Authority has formulated a plan to import 1,154 megawatts of electricity from India. Amid declining domestic generation and rising demand, this import has been made the primary foundation for supply management.
 According to the NEA’s plan, preparations are underway to bring 600 megawatts from the Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur 400 kV transmission line, 54 megawatts from the Tanakpur-Mahendranagar 132 kV transmission line, and 350 megawatts from various transmission points in Bihar. In addition, there is a plan to purchase an extra 150 megawatts through the real-time market (RTC) system. Combining the electricity from all these sources brings total imports to 1,154 megawatts.
 NEA Executive Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha has stated that because domestic generation alone cannot meet demand in the winter, plans have been made to import electricity from India. According to the NEA’s estimates, combining 1,218 megawatts of domestic generation with 1,154 megawatts of imports will make about 2,372 megawatts of electricity available in the system.
 Making plans to import electricity from India and having as much electricity available as needed when required are two different things.
 “The suspension of generation from projects in the Trishuli river system has created some pressure on demand and supply management. However, there will be no load-shedding this winter. We have initiated preparations right from now for a reliable electricity supply,” Shrestha stated.
 Last winter, Nepal’s peak electricity demand reached approximately 2,292 megawatts. Based on estimates that demand will remain around that level this year, the NEA assesses that demand can be met through a combination of imports and domestic generation. However, this estimate depends on the actual availability of supplied electricity and the operational capacity of the system.
 Making plans to import electricity from India and having as much electricity available as needed when required are two different things. Nepal must coordinate with India’s electricity power market, its production conditions, demand, and available transmission system capacity. Since electricity demand also rises in India during the winter, ensuring that electricity is made available in the quantities and at the times requested by Nepal is crucial.
 India has granted Nepal permission to export up to 654 megawatts of electricity daily for now, with this authorization valid until December 31.
 Managing supply can be especially challenging during peak evening demand hours. When demand from residential use, industries, commercial establishments, and other services surges simultaneously, it puts pressure on the system. Under such conditions, if imported electricity drops or disruptions occur in the transmission system, domestic generation alone will struggle to meet immediate demand.
 India has granted Nepal permission to export up to 654 megawatts of electricity daily for now, with this authorization valid until December 31. The volume of electricity to be exported starting January 2027 will be reviewed by India in December. The current permission covers the period from midnight to 6:00 PM. The lack of guaranteed imports during peak evening demand hours poses another challenge for Nepal’s supply management.
 The success of the NEA’s import plan is one of the main foundations for preventing load-shedding.
 Import approvals, purchase agreements, transmission line availability, and power market conditions must all operate in tandem. Therefore, the success of the NEA’s import plan is one of the main foundations for preventing load-shedding. Even if import volumes are secured on paper, if transmission infrastructure fails to deliver electricity at the required time, its practical utility cannot be realized.
 Heavy damage to the energy sector from floods and landslides 
 Floods and landslides during this year’s monsoon caused severe damage to Nepal’s energy sector. Floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems damaged hydropower projects, access roads, transmission lines, and other infrastructure. Subsequently, continuous rainfall and landslides in various areas affected additional projects and transmission structures.
 Floods in the Bhotekoshi region directly impacted hydropower projects located in Rasuwa and surrounding districts. Some projects were fully affected, while major damage was inflicted on certain under-construction projects and transmission structures. As roads, bridges, and other access infrastructure leading to project sites were damaged, repair and restoration work has also become difficult.
 According to the World Bank’s Global Rapid Post-Disaster Damage Estimation report, floods on August 26 affected seven operational hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 256.1 megawatts. Similarly, the capacity of five under-construction projects totaling 395.02 megawatts was affected. The report noted that a 25-megawatt solar project was also damaged.
 The preliminary damage and needs assessment prepared by a joint technical team from the government’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and the National Planning Commission also shows that damage to the energy sector is severe.
 Damage to transmission infrastructure created bottlenecks in bringing an additional 149.6 megawatts of electricity into the grid, the report details. This shows that the impact of the floods was not limited to generation centers alone, extending to power transmission and supply.
 The preliminary damage and needs assessment prepared by a joint technical team from the government’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and the National Planning Commission also shows that damage to the energy sector is severe. The assessment notes that 13 hydropower projects and five solar projects were affected, with the combined capacity of the hydropower projects standing at 759 megawatts and the solar projects at 24 megawatts.
 Government estimates indicate that approximately Rs 390.62 billion will be required solely for the restoration of the energy and grid systems. This estimated amount covers not only the reconstruction of hydropower projects but also the restoration of transmission, distribution, substations, and other energy infrastructure.
 If production from flood-affected projects fails to resume on time, even the estimated volume of domestic generation could decrease.
 Judging by the scale of the damage, the impact on the energy sector cannot be resolved through routine maintenance alone; several projects require reconstruction. When transmission towers, access roads, and riverside structures are damaged, connecting power generation to the national grid becomes problematic even if a project resumes generation.
 NEA Spokesperson Rajan Dhakal stated that the damage caused by floods could be significantly larger than preliminary estimates. According to him, rescue operations, the search for missing persons, and the restoration of electricity supply are immediate priorities.
 “Right now, our priority is rescue, the search for missing persons, and restoring electricity supply. There has been unimaginable loss of life and property. According to our preliminary estimates, damages could reach hundreds of billions of rupees,” Dhakal says. This has a direct impact on winter supply. If production from flood-affected projects fails to resume on time, even the estimated volume of domestic generation could decrease, potentially necessitating higher electricity imports from India or creating additional pressure on demand management.
 Nepal Electricity Authority. File photo
 Production means little when transmission lines are weak 
 Nepal’s energy sector has long focused heavily on generation capacity. The construction of new hydropower projects and the expansion of installed capacity are presented as achievements. However, transmission and distribution infrastructure, which connects generated electricity to the national grid and delivers it to consumers, is equally vital.
 Floods and landslides have exposed the vulnerabilities of this very infrastructure. When riverside hydropower projects, transmission towers, and access roads are placed at risk, both generation and supply are affected. In some instances, even when projects are operational, blocked transmission lines prevent electricity from reaching markets.
 The World Bank’s evaluation notes that in addition to affecting production, damage to transmission infrastructure has also created bottlenecks in the power system.
 The damage sustained in the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river systems this year demonstrates how critical the relationship between generation and transmission is. The World Bank’s evaluation notes that in addition to affecting production, damage to transmission infrastructure has also created bottlenecks in the power system.
 According to Hitendra Dev Shakya, former executive director of the Nepal Electricity Authority, rebuilding damaged projects in their old formats is inappropriate. He suggests designing new structures by taking flood risks, river flows, and potential glacial lake outburst floods into account.
 “The mindset of rebuilding old structures exactly as they were should not be entertained. Learning from the current disaster, we must change designs keeping new risks in mind,” Shakya stated. According to him, building powerhouses in areas prone to river flooding is risky. Wherever possible, underground powerhouses, safe shelters, and emergency exit arrangements should be established.
 The authority has also prioritized the option of bringing electricity imported from India into the Kathmandu Valley via the Dhalkebar-Hetauda 400 kV transmission line.
 As electricity demand continues to rise in the Kathmandu Valley, expanding the capacity of transmission and distribution infrastructure has become even more essential. The NEA is preparing to manage the valley’s power distribution system through the Chobhar, Phutung, and Mulpani substations. A plan has been advanced to ease supply by transferring the load carried by old substations and feeders onto new structures.
 The NEA has also prioritized the option of bringing electricity imported from India into the Kathmandu Valley via the Dhalkebar-Hetauda 400 kV transmission line. This is expected to help improve power supply and reduce voltage issues in the valley.
 If electricity demand rises but distribution system capacity is not expanded accordingly, increasing production and imports alone will not solve the problem.
 NEA Executive Director Shrestha stated that preparations are underway to utilize new substations and distribution structures for managing demand in the Kathmandu Valley. Peak demand in the valley reached about 700 megawatts last winter, and the NEA estimates it could increase by roughly 10 percent this year.
 If electricity demand rises but distribution system capacity is not expanded accordingly, increasing production and imports alone will not solve the problem. Excessive loads on old feeders, transformers, and substations in the valley can cause localized power interruptions. Consequently, improving the distribution system alongside generation has become an immediate challenge for the NEA.
 Managing peak demand through Kulekhani 
 Because electricity generation declines in winter, the role of storage-type projects becomes crucial. Even when river flows drop in run-of-the-river projects, water stored in reservoirs can be utilized according to needs and demand. Therefore, storage projects help manage peak evening demand.
 The Kulekhani Hydropower Project is a vital resource of this kind within Nepal’s electricity system. The NEA has planned to utilize water available in the Kulekhani reservoir systematically to increase generation during peak demand hours. Plans are in place to operate all three units as needed to manage evening demand.
 The NEA has attempted to make up for the shortfall in generation by continuously operating all three phases of the 106-megawatt Kulekhani reservoir project.
 However, Kulekhani’s capacity is limited. Once stored water in the reservoir is used, it takes time to refill. Therefore, high generation cannot be sustained continuously throughout the entire winter. Decisions regarding when to use the reservoir’s water must be made by evaluating power demand, generation from other projects, and import conditions.
 Following the floods, Kulekhani has had to be utilized beyond normal operational levels. The NEA has attempted to make up for the shortfall in generation by continuously operating all three phases of the 106-megawatt Kulekhani reservoir project. Kulekhani, which is normally preserved to maintain reserves for the winter, has had to be drawn down more heavily to stabilize the system following the floods. This increases the risk of placing pressure on available winter reservoir storage reserves.
 Energy sector experts have long pointed out that constructing storage-type projects is necessary to reduce the seasonal imbalance between power demand and generation in Nepal.
 Former Executive Director Kulman Ghising stated that the floods have provided a lesson on improving the design and safety arrangements of hydropower projects. According to him, structures protecting powerhouses from floods, early warning systems, and emergency rescue arrangements must be incorporated directly into project designs.
 “Hydropower projects must be designed to withstand floods. Early warning systems and effective emergency rescue arrangements are necessary. By making access tunnels leading to powerhouses longer, they can be protected from floodwaters,” says Ghising.
 The inability to increase the number of storage-type projects like Kulekhani represents another weakness in Nepal’s energy security. Because run-of-the-river projects have high generation in the wet season and low generation in winter, the seasonal production gap will persist until sufficient storage projects are built.
 Constructing such projects requires massive investment, long timeframes, environmental studies, land management, and local-level consensus.
 Energy sector experts have long pointed out that constructing storage-type projects is necessary to reduce the seasonal imbalance between power demand and generation in Nepal. However, constructing such projects requires massive investment, long timeframes, environmental studies, land management, and local-level consensus. Therefore, the immediate problem of winter supply cannot be solved solely by operating Kulekhani.
 Risks associated with reliance on Indian supply 
 Symbolic photo.
 Nepal has developed a system where it exports electricity during the rainy season and imports it during winter. From the perspective of regional power trade, this may be a natural arrangement. However, needing to import a large share of the electricity required to meet peak national demand from a single neighboring country can be risky from an energy security standpoint.
 When importing electricity from India, factors such as price, timing, transmission capacity, and approvals are critical. As supply and demand conditions shift in the power market, purchase prices can also change. If Nepal cannot purchase electricity when needed or if supplies fall short of expected volumes, the impact is felt directly in domestic supply.
 This year, the NEA has planned to import 1,154 megawatts of electricity. However, securing this volume requires electricity to be made available through various transmission routes. Along with plans to bring 600 megawatts via the Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur transmission line, 350 megawatts from various points in Bihar, and 54 megawatts from Tanakpur, the process of purchasing 150 megawatts through the RTC is also crucial.
 While diversifying import sources is positive, the necessary transmission infrastructure and purchase agreements must be secured on time. If problems arise on one transmission route, the capacity to divert power through alternative routes is required. Recent events where floods and landslides damaged transmission infrastructure have further highlighted the need for such contingency arrangements.
 While exporting surplus electricity during the rainy season is necessary, it should not undermine domestic energy demand and consumption targets.
 On the other hand, although Nepal earns revenue from electricity exports during the wet season, it must spend heavily on imports during the winter. While this seasonal trade helps manage immediate supply, it is not proof of long-term energy self-reliance. Unless boosting domestic generation in winter and constructing storage projects are prioritized, import dependency will persist.
 Mohan Das Manandhar, president of the Nepal Energy Foundation, expressed the view that rather than stopping exports entirely, domestic consumption should be prioritized within seasonal power trading. According to him, while exporting surplus electricity during the rainy season is necessary, it should not undermine domestic energy demand and consumption targets.
 “Electricity export is necessary to manage the gap between seasonal production and demand. But that does not mean putting domestic consumption in the background. Exports and domestic consumption must be advanced in a balanced manner,” Manandhar opines.
 Long-term planning required alongside reconstruction 
 The damage inflicted on the energy sector by floods and landslides cannot be resolved through immediate repairs alone. Substantial investment is required to restore damaged projects and transmission infrastructure. According to government assessments, approximately Rs 390.62 billion will be needed to restore the energy and grid systems. This figure highlights not only the physical magnitude of the damage but also the challenge of rebuilding energy infrastructure.
 When reconstructing, rather than rebuilding old structures exactly as they were, future flood and landslide risks must be taken into account. Riverside projects, transmission towers, substations, and access roads must be made secure against natural disaster risks. Otherwise, there is a risk that identical damage will repeat every monsoon, with impacts extending all the way to winter power supplies.
 According to Uttam Bholon Lama, senior vice president of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), floods caused greater damage to older, surface-level powerhouses. He noted that newer projects suffered relatively less damage because their underground powerhouses and desilting structures were built underground.
 “Newer projects featuring underground powerhouses and desilting structures suffered relatively less damage. Overall, we estimate damages at 25 to 30 percent of total project costs, though full evaluations remain pending,” Lama stated.
 The government must formulate river basin-based planning regarding where projects should be built on which river systems.
 Recent events have highlighted the necessity of incorporating climate and disaster risks into energy sector planning right from the start. The World Bank report noted that floods in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river systems caused massive physical damage and altered river flows, bank erosion, and topography. This shows that risk assessments for projects and transmission infrastructure should not be limited to conventional technical studies.
 Arjun Dhakal, an environmental and climate change economist, stated that risk assessments for hydropower projects should evaluate entire river systems rather than single projects in isolation. He argued that despite the high number of operational and under-construction projects in the Trishuli region, the cumulative risks to the river have not received adequate attention.
 “Because projects were permitted for haphazard construction along river corridors without considering natural risks such as glacial lake outburst floods originating from Tibet, the damage was massive,” Dhakal said. According to him, the government must formulate river basin-based planning regarding where projects should be built on which river systems.
 Encouraging industries and large consumers to manage the timing of their electricity consumption, increasing distribution system capacity, and adopting alternative management during peak demand hours can reduce system pressure.
 Deepak KC, an expert who has worked on disaster risk reduction and the safety of hydropower structures, also stated that climate and disaster risks should be incorporated across all four phases of project development. According to him, studies on potential floods, glacial lake outburst floods, landslides, and river flow risks must be conducted before issuing permits.
 “Technology can be effectively used to mitigate risks across all four stages of hydropower projects: surveying, design, construction, and operation,” KC stated. According to him, in addition to developing an integrated information system for glaciers, rainfall, and river flows, risk reduction systems based on river corridors are necessary.
 To transform the achievements Nepal has made in expanding hydropower generation into long-term energy security, the pattern of generation must also change. Increasing investments in storage-type projects, pumped storage, energy storage, and regional transmission infrastructure alongside run-of-the-river projects is necessary. Developing a system that can utilize electricity that would otherwise go to waste or be exported at low prices during the rainy season in winter is equally vital.
 According to the NEA’s estimates, combining 1,218 megawatts of domestic generation with 1,154 megawatts of imports will provide approximately 2,372 megawatts of electricity.
 Similarly, attention must be directed toward electricity demand management. Encouraging industries and large consumers to manage the timing of their electricity consumption, increasing distribution system capacity, and adopting alternative management during peak demand hours can reduce system pressure.
 Will load-shedding return or not? 
 The answer to whether load-shedding will occur this winter cannot be stated with absolute certainty right now. The NEA has estimated that demand can be met by combining domestic generation and electricity imported from India. However, for that estimate to hold true, import plans must be implemented, damaged projects and transmission structures must be operationalized on time, and the power distribution system must be able to sustain peak demand.
 According to the NEA’s estimates, combining 1,218 megawatts of domestic generation with 1,154 megawatts of imports will provide approximately 2,372 megawatts of electricity. This volume exceeds last year’s peak demand. However, the timing of demand, transmission bottlenecks, project restoration status, and import regularity will determine actual supplies.
 Therefore, the NEA’s claim that load-shedding will not occur cannot be evaluated solely on the aggregate arithmetic of generation and imports. The core question is whether required volumes will be available during peak demand hours. Even if sufficient electricity exists in the system, if bottlenecks occur in transmission or distribution infrastructure, consumers will not receive a regular supply.
 To safeguard the achievement of ending load-shedding, Nepal must implement long-term energy planning alongside immediate supply management. Relying solely on winter imports from India and wet-season exports will not fulfill energy security goals. Reducing the seasonal imbalance in domestic generation, constructing storage-type projects, expanding transmission infrastructure, and developing disaster-resilient energy systems must now be the priority.
 Nepal has made remarkable progress in electricity generation. However, the persistence of an inability to meet domestic demand in winter and the recurring threat posed by floods and landslides to energy infrastructure show that this progress does not yet stand on a secure foundation. Preventing load-shedding this winter will be an immediate success. But building a reliable, secure, and self-reliant electricity system by reducing dependency on Indian imports over the long term is Nepal’s true test.
